text: TRANSCRIPT REFERENCE B-ROLL TIME TRT POWER IS EXPENSIVE: Adam Richins – 04;17;00 “Over the last, 15 years, our rates have average gone up 1.2% a year. That's quite a bit less than inflation. Now, we don't love that 1.2%. It's something we're trying not to do. But when you look at CPI compared to that it's still pretty low. And our generally are 20 to 30% below the national average.” Pg. 5 Adam Richins – 04;45;00 “Now this last year, we did have a rate increase. It ended up being settled at about 7%. So that may be what some folks are talking about. That rate case did not have any dollars related to large load infrastructure because they pay for that all upfront.” Pg. 5 Jim Buie – CLIP X Adam Richins – 07;47;00 “A lot of it is onshoring. So manufacturing, like micron and others coming back, to the United States or growing in the United States. We have new mining loads. We have new food processing, food manufacturing. It's really, really diverse. And that makes up the large chunk of it, in addition to new pumps in farming from irrigators.” Pg. 9 AGRICULTURE IS FEELING IT: Andrew Mickelsen – 18;14;00 “As farmers, we've been here. The power usage has been here for the last 50 years. Why are we having to pay more? All of a sudden? Why are we having to subsidize that new company that's coming in?” Pg. 18 Adam Richins – 02;04;00 “Idaho has been very strict on this mantra of growth pays for growth. So if you're going to come for our service territory, that's great. We have really low rates. You need to pay your way and make sure those costs aren't spread to other customers.” Pg. 3 Adam Richins – “In Idaho. There's an entire process. It's actually a litigated process. It goes to our commissioners.” Pg.3 Andrew Mickelsen – 21;13;00 “This group is costing this much, this group is costing this much. And so then they propose increases based upon that agriculture. You're going to go up 13%. Commercial is going to go up 8% or whatever it is. And then we all come. When we look at the studies, we make sure there's no flaws in that methodology and come back together at the end and say, okay, without litigating this, maybe we can adjust these a little bit.” Pg.20 HOW THE PUC PROCESS WORKS: Adam Richins – 02;45;00 “We put forward what we think the right rate is for different, large load customers based on their cost to the system. It is then evaluated. Sometimes that process takes anywhere from nine months to a year. So it's pretty significant. Other customers that may be impacted can intervene. They bring lawyers and other interested parties to push back and to really compromise and agree on what we think that that cost is. And then ultimately, the commissioners make the decision,” Pg. 3 Adam Richins – 03;34;06 “it's a public process. Any party, that wants to intervene, that has representation can intervene. In terms of what is kept, you know, confidential. Every now and then there'll be there's information that may be proprietary, the commissioners will still see it, and a lot of the parties can still see it.” Pg. 4 Andrew Mickelsen – 12;24;00 “They always have a good reason. They always have something that's why, you know, inflation is hitting. We all know that. Go to the grocery store. Things cost more. There are costs that are going up the supplies that it takes to fix and repair power lines. I know it's costing more” Pg. 13 Jim Buie – CLIP X IDAHO POWER IS ALWAYS ON: Jim Buie and site tour footage X Adam Richins – 00;37;00 “You don't really store electricity once it's generated. It's balanced in real time. You have to make sure the demand is equal to supply at all times, 24 hours a day, seven days a week.” Pg.1 Adam Richins – 01;26;00 “I'm not sure necessarily how other states deal with data centers, large loads. There's been a lot of articles out there saying that they increase costs for others. What we're worried about is Idaho, and Idaho has a pretty defined process where these entities, when they come and want a site here, they have to pay a large amount of the infrastructure costs to do that upfront.” Pg. 2 WHY BUILD A LARGE LOAD IN IDAHO: Jim Bue – CLIP X Adam Richins – 01;09;00 “So as these manufacturers come to Idaho, use more energy. We obviously have to plan for them, make sure we have the generation resources available, make sure we have the transmission and distribution infrastructure available for them. And so it's a pretty significant planning process. We spend a lot of our days doing that.” Pg. 2 Andrew Mickelsen – 13;51;00 “That's something that has us very worried. What we've seen is a lot of data centers looking at Idaho, or even big manufacturing, such as micron looking Idaho and saying, hey, this could be a great place to go to. Power is pretty, pretty cost effective. And we have a lot of green energy in the state. And one of the things that these data centers or productions looked at is we want to be able to show that we're using green power, that we're using power that's coming from renewable sources.” Pg. 14 Adam Richins – 03;14;00 “It's not necessarily the irrigators or, residential customers or even Idaho Power that decides what those rates should be. And are these customers paying their fair share for the system? There, is evidence that's put forward. The commissioners review that evidence, and then they make a decision, based on what they're seeing.” Pg. 4 PUBLIC PERCEPTION OF DATA CENTERS: Andrew Mickelsen – 14;50;00 “It is great to see businesses coming to the state, and we do want to encourage that growth. You know, the company that comes in and it's employing 100 500 people, thousand people. Yeah. You want that. You want to see that in our state. But at the same time, should the cost be borne by everybody else? And a lot of those people might not have those benefits. I don't think that the rate payers in general should have to be subsidizing a potato processing plant or a micron, but especially not a data center.” Pg. 15 Jim Buie – CLIP X Adam Richins – 01;52;00 “Different substations, transmission lines, distribution lines, a variety of different, equipment that's going to serve directly these entities. They pay upfront for that. So those costs aren't spread to other customers.” Pg. 3 Andrew Mickelsen – 17;05;00 “They have done a great job, providing power, being a public utility. But as we're seeing these huge demands come in. We're seeing sweetheart deals. It just becomes problematic as their motivations can become misaligned.” Pg. 17 IS CHANGING LAWS WHAT IS NEEDED: Adam Richins – 06;19;00 “You see legislation coming in other states because they don't have this no harm process. Idaho does have it. [Why] interfere with that? It's been really successful. So far. I mean, our rates are again, if you look across a map, our rates are the lowest in the nation. In Idaho, these processes have been a part of that. So let's keep these processes in place and rely on them as we move forward.” Pg. 7 Andrew Mickelsen – 17;21;00 “They go put out more money to meet these new customers that they give lower rates to. They still get the same return, and I'm afraid that it's just shifting from one ratepayer class to another.” Pg. 17 Andrew Mickelsen – 17;46;00 “They don't want to be saying what they're paying or what they're requiring a meter or a micron to pay. They want to keep that quiet, because if you, as a consumer knew that you were paying three, four times as much as these data centers, you'd probably start seeing, wait, what's going on here?” Pg. 17 Jim Buie – CLIP X LEGISLATIVE LANDSCAPE AS SESSION ENDS: Adam Richins – 08;58;00 “Energy has become pretty political, and you'll hear people say, you know, I know power should build all renewables. And certainly there's a group of people that believes that you're going to hear another group of people say, I know power should build, you know, fossil fuels and natural gas and coal. What the engineering and what the models show. And this is all part of a public process, the integrated resource plan. You can click on our website and you can see this document. We run these very sophisticated models that look at every hour and every day and tell us what resources idle power should actually build, what transmission, what generation resources we should build, what the models show is the truth is somewhere in the middle.” Pg. 10 Andrew Mickelsen – 18;31;00 “Those deals should not be done in backrooms. They should be out there publicly. Because if you can't publicly justify why you're giving that power at a fraction of the rate that you are, then you are to others, that's a problem.” Pg. 18 Adam Richins – 00;08;00 “But what I think people don't understand in our service territory is data centers are actually a smaller percentage of that. A lot of people are hearing it nationally. So they're assuming our growth is data centers. For us it's not the smaller portion of it is data centers. The rest of it is residential large loads, irrigation, small businesses, you know, commercial entities that are growing. And we're seeing that growth and it's pretty significant.” Pg. 9 A-ROLL B-ROLL TIME TRT
